cim: How To Ensure Artificial Intelligence Is Enriching Student Learning
cim_eredeti: How To Ensure Artificial Intelligence Is Enriching Student Learning
szoveg_eredeti:
When Wichita Public Schools began exploring generative artificial intelligence in January 2023, the goal was simple: to save teachers some time. By April, it had become something bigger. District leaders saw a chance to design personalized learning experiences for students, and they have built on that idea ever since.

“There was an instant shift,” says Dyane Smokorowski, coordinator of digital literacy at Wichita Public Schools. “This is a way that we can start purposely designing for students with learning differences. This is a way that we can start designing for those in the margins versus designing for the middle and hoping that the margins can come into play. That’s been our driving force.”

A Brookings Institution study from earlier this year describes what AI-enriched learning looks like when tools are used within a sound approach to teaching. Its Prosper, Prepare and Protect framework gives schools a roadmap for getting there. WPS shows how a district can follow it, from building teacher confidence to supporting every learner, while it keeps refining how to measure what’s working.

The Brookings Institution notes that AI should transform learning experiences to help students thrive. The report says AI should be used to deepen learning, not replace the effort it takes to get there. This effort is how students learn, Smokorowski says.

“Students still need to have productive struggle,” she says. “It is good for their brains. It is good for them as humans. So, how do we design while keeping thinking at the center in an AI world?”

At WPS, the approach is to use AI to build supports for students while maintaining expectations for learning.

Katelyn Schoenhofer, technology instructional coach at WPS, says the district recognizes two kinds of support. Scaffolds are temporary, and teachers gradually remove them as students build skills, so the goal is independence. Accommodations are supports that some students will always need, and they are designed so the student still does the thinking. In both cases, the expectation stays the same. The risk with traditional accommodations is that they sometimes end up changing the expectation, Schoenhofer says.

Teachers know how to create these supports, but doing it for every student and every need is more than anyone can manage. AI gives teachers back their time, taking over their administrative work, which leaves teachers free to deliver supports in person.

The district is now extending this to paraprofessionals, training them on how AI can help them support students in one-on-one or small group settings. Paras know individual students well and can build visual guides and other supports for them.

“We have another opportunity to meet the needs of these children in a personalized way that we have never been able to do before,” Smokorowski says. “Many paras come with different digital skill sets than teachers. They just haven't had the opportunity to learn. We were very quick to discover that they are becoming more confident in supporting their students." She adds that training the paraprofessionals has only started, so the outcomes are yet to be seen.

LEARN MORE: AI literacy requires students to stay curious about how the tech works.

Many districts are tackling AI readiness by promoting AI literacy for both students and teachers. The Brookings Institution recommends adequate training for teachers to ensure they are equipped to use AI responsibly and model the critical thinking skills students will need.

At WPS, teachers receive this training first; student modeling follows once teachers understand the technology.

“As teachers become more comfortable with what it does for them, they are able to have those conversations with students, to really get students familiar with what AI can do and what it should do,” Schoenhofer says. That took time, she says, as teachers themselves had to understand AI’s purpose in supporting their work rather than simply doing it for them.

For students, WPS has adopted grade-banded expectations for AI use and exposure, Schoenhofer says.

In kindergarten through first grade, teachers simply talk with students about AI and avoid personifying it. In second through fifth grades, students still have no independent exposure to AI, though teachers might model it themselves so students can see how it works. In grades six through eight, students can use a few approved tools, but they don’t have access to writing capabilities. Teachers also begin digital citizenship lessons on how AI works, what is safe and appropriate, and where AI falls short. In high school, the focus shifts to critically analyzing AI outputs and deciding when using AI supports productive struggle and when it undermines it.

“We've built a lot of our guidelines and policies off of what the surrounding universities have done,” Schoenhofer says. “They're not banning AI. They are putting in restrictions on how you use it, making sure that you're sharing your conversations and being explicit and transparent about it. We're asking teachers to be transparent with students so that students can see how it's used, and then we're asking students how they might use it and what are some different ways that it could support them.”

DISCOVER: AI-ready classrooms start with data governance, policy and training.

Once the teaching and learning goals are defined and students are prepared, it’s vital for schools to protect children from the adverse impacts of AI. Brookings Institution recommends age-appropriate AI experiences with reasonable guardrails while also fostering strong human relationships. They also recommend educating families to ensure responsible AI use continues at home.

At WPS, educators address the protection element early, in the kindergarten through first grade band. Students are taught that AI is a robot that works from patterns, that its answers need to be double-checked, and that it is not a friend or someone to turn to with problems.

Schoenhofer says AI’s infancy offers districts an opportunity to get ahead of potential bad habits that students might adopt. With other areas of technology, such as social media, schools have had to identify bad habits, break them down and rebuild better ones.

“We have an amazing opportunity that we haven't had with technology before,” she says. “With AI, if we're proactive now, they don't have those bad habits yet. If we can get out in front of that, we don't have to break down and then rebuild. We can just start building from the beginning. I'm really excited about this opportunity, and I hope that other districts see that we have to lead the way instead of waiting.”

While districts grapple with how to tackle this issue, Smokorowski notes that collaboration can ease the load.

“We don't have to do this alone,” she says. “We need to do this in partnership, district to district. If you're a district that's exploring what the possibilities could be, don't do this on your own. Find others who are taking the lead, and let's do this together.”
